## Circular to Licensed Corporations

## Window Dressing of Financial Position

In the past, the SFC has detected a number of cases involving 'window dressing' of financial position by brokers. Window dressing is a dishonest act, which the SFC will not tolerate.

## Securities  and  Futures  (Financial  Resources)  Rules  (FRRs)  are  cornerstone  of prudential regulation

The FRRs are designed to ensure that brokers have sufficient funds to operate their business  and  meet  liabilities.  Brokers  are  required  to  maintain  a  minimum  level  of liquid capital at all times and to lodge monthly financial returns with the SFC. The FRRs  are  the  central  cornerstone  for  prudential  regulation  as  they  are  designed  to ensure that brokers have sufficient liquid capital to conduct their business in a prudent manner for market confidence.

In addition, the law requires a broker to notify the SFC and cease dealing in securities upon failure to meet the FRRs. It is therefore very important for a broker that is not able to comply with the FRRs to advise the SFC immediately so that we can work with the broker to address the risks and overcome difficulties.

## Window dressing of financial position

Window dressing is the act of telling lies or using cover-up schemes to camouflage a firm's  real  financial  position.  It  often  includes  unusual  fund  transfers  with  related parties, understatement of liabilities and fictitious transactions, etc. Sometimes, it may involve falsification of financial records or misappropriation of client monies, which is  criminal. Such activities seriously impugn the fitness and propernesss of the firm and the integrity of its management.

## SFC regulatory actions

Window dressing raises two principal concerns. Firstly, it raises issues of fitness and properness  of  the  broker,  and  whether  the  broker  should  be  allowed  to  continue business,  or  to  continue  in  any  particular  manner,  given  the  underlying  integrity issues.

Secondly,  it  raises  the  equally  fundamental  question  of  whether  the  broker  is financially  sound,  and  if  it  has  sufficient  liquid  capital  to  continue  its  business without posing any risks to its clients and investors.

Depending on the seriousness and circumstances of the problem, the SFC may use a combination of measures to protect the integrity of the market and the interests of clients  and  investors.  These  include  both  enforcement  actions,  such  as  public reprimand, suspension or revocation of licence, and prudential measures to manage down  financial  risks.    Where  necessary,  the  SFC  may  apply  to  the  Court  for  the appointment of an administrator to administer and preserve the broker's properties.

Window dressing does not only affect the broker itself, it is also detrimental to the reputation of the whole industry. The SFC believes that the majority of the brokerage industry are law abiding, but a few might be tempted to believe, rather wrongly, that they could get away with window dressing activities.  We would like to emphasise that  the  SFC  will  take  all  necessary  actions  against  any  misconduct  which  may jeopardise the market integrity and the interest of the investing public.
